title: Time series: wide-column with TWCS, a time-series database, or a data lake?

rows.label: In one line
values: One partition per series and time bucket, rows sorted by time, old windows dropped as whole files
A database built around timestamped points: time chunks, specialised compression, retention and rollups
Columnar files in object storage, partitioned by date and read by any SQL engine

rows.label: Write path
values: Each point is a row appended to the commit log and memtable on every replica, later flushed to SSTables
Points go into the newest time chunk or an in-memory head, which is cut into blocks (two hours in Prometheus)
Points are batched by a stream or batch job and written as new files, such as Parquet, under a date folder

rows.label: How old data expires
values: A TTL per row; with TWCS, an SSTable whose rows have all expired is deleted whole, unless it might shadow older data
A retention setting drops whole blocks or chunks past an age (15 days by default in Prometheus; `add_retention_policy` in TimescaleDB)
Lifecycle rules delete files by age or move them to archive storage such as S3 Glacier; or a job drops old date partitions

rows.label: Latest value per series
values: Fast: the first row of the series’ current partition (`LIMIT 1` with `ts DESC`)
Built in: a PromQL instant query returns the newest sample of every matching series
Slow: scan the newest partitions and keep the highest timestamp per key; there is no index

rows.label: Time range for one series
values: The query it is designed for: one partition per bucket, read in clustering order
Fast: chunks outside the time range are skipped
Date partitions outside the range are skipped, but each remaining file is scanned for the series

rows.label: Aggregates across all series
values: Weak: `GROUP BY` works only on primary key columns, and filtering across partitions is a full scan; usually a separate rollup table or a Spark job
The main job: aggregation over series and time windows, plus background rollups such as TimescaleDB continuous aggregates
Good: engines read only the columns a query needs, across as much history as you keep

rows.label: Ad-hoc analytics
values: Poor: every query must follow the partition key; a new question needs a new table or an external engine such as Spark or Trino
Depends on the language: full SQL with joins in TimescaleDB, series and labels only in PromQL
Its strength: schema on read, and any engine (Athena, Trino, Spark, DuckDB) over the same files

rows.label: Compression
values: General-purpose, per SSTable: LZ4 on 16 KiB chunks by default, Zstd for a better ratio
Per-column encodings for time series (delta-of-delta, XOR, run-length): Prometheus averages 1–2 bytes per sample; TimescaleDB’s columnstore saves more than 90%
Columnar files with per-column compression; Athena reads only the columns a query names

rows.label: Keeping years of history
values: Costly: every replica keeps the data on its own disks, and the node count grows with it
Cheaper after compression and rollups; Prometheus’s local storage isn’t replicated, so long-term data goes to a remote store
Cheapest: object storage billed per GB-month, with archive tiers; queries pay per data scanned ($5 per TB in Athena)

rows.label: Typical products
values: Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Amazon Keyspaces; Bigtable expires cells by age through per-column-family garbage collection instead
TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, Prometheus, QuestDB, kdb+
S3, Azure Data Lake Storage or Cloud Storage with Parquet, queried by Athena, Trino or Spark

tip: They answer different questions, and many systems use two of them. Use a wide-column store with TWCS when an application reads per series, such as a device’s latest reading or its last day, at high write rates and across regions, and you can live without ad-hoc queries. Use a time-series database when most reads are dashboards and aggregates over many series and recent time. Use a data lake for years of history and questions nobody has asked yet: it is the cheapest place to keep data, but the slowest for one series or one latest value. A common split is to stream the same events into Cassandra with a 30-day TTL for the application and into Parquet files for analysis.
